title: Reunification, 1989–1991
description: Gorbachev's reforms, the collapse of the GDR, the fall of the Wall, Kohl's Ten-Point Plan and the road to October 1990.
content_html:
Gorbachev's Reforms and Their Impact on East Germany

The revolution that ended the GDR began not in East Germany but in Moscow. When Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985, he introduced two transformative policies. Glasnost (openness) allowed greater freedom of expression in the Soviet Union; perestroika (restructuring) attempted to reform the Soviet economy. Crucially, Gorbachev signalled that the Soviet Union would no longer use military force to maintain communist governments in Eastern Europe — a reversal of the Brezhnev Doctrine, which had justified Soviet intervention in Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968). This decision meant that Eastern European regimes no longer had Soviet tanks as their ultimate guarantor of survival.

Erich Honecker, the GDR's leader, rejected Gorbachev's reforms, insisting they were inappropriate for East Germany. The GDR's official newspaper refused to distribute a Soviet magazine that contained reform-minded articles. This growing divergence between Moscow and East Berlin left the SED increasingly isolated — it was committed to a hard-line course that even the Soviet Union was abandoning.

Key Fact

Gorbachev's key decision was to refuse to use Soviet military force to save communist regimes in Eastern Europe. Without this backstop, the SED could not rely on Soviet tanks to crush popular opposition as they had in 1953. This made the regime fundamentally vulnerable in 1989.

The 1989 Revolutions Across Eastern Europe

The year 1989 brought a cascade of revolutions across the communist bloc. In Poland, partially free elections in June 1989 produced a crushing defeat for the communist party; in Hungary, reforms opened the border with Austria in May 1989 — a critical development for East Germans. Hungary's open border provided a new escape route: East Germans on holiday in Hungary could cross into Austria and then travel to West Germany. By September 1989 approximately 30,000 East Germans had taken this route. Others sought refuge in West German embassies in Prague and Warsaw, which became scenes of mass occupation as East Germans camped in the embassy gardens waiting for exit permits.

The Monday Demonstrations in Leipzig

While tens of thousands were fleeing, others decided to stay and demand change. Every Monday evening, East Germans gathered for demonstrations in Leipzig — originally for prayers at the Nikolaikirche (St Nicholas Church) that turned into political protests. The Monday Demonstrations grew rapidly: from hundreds in September 1989 to approximately 70,000 on 9 October 1989. That Monday was a moment of acute tension — some SED officials had discussed using force to clear the demonstrators, and there were reports of hospital staff being placed on alert. The demonstration passed peacefully, however, and the crisis passed without a Tiananmen Square-style crackdown. The following Monday, 16 October, brought approximately 120,000 demonstrators.

Under pressure from the protests and from within the SED, Erich Honecker was ousted on 18 October 1989 and replaced by Egon Krenz. The SED attempted to manage the crisis — partly by announcing reforms and partly by trying to control the flow of information. On 9 November 1989, a confused press conference announcement by SED spokesman Günter Schabowski — who had not been briefed on the intended limits of new travel rules — led thousands of East Berliners to converge on the border crossings demanding to be let through. Overwhelmed guards, without clear orders, opened the gates. The Berlin Wall fell on the night of 9 November 1989.

Helmut Kohl and the Ten-Point Plan

West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl seized the initiative. On 28 November 1989 — less than three weeks after the Wall fell — he announced a Ten-Point Plan for the gradual reunification of Germany, without prior consultation with his Western allies or Gorbachev. The plan envisaged a phased approach: first expanded cooperation between the two Germanies, then a confederal arrangement, and eventually full unification. Kohl moved far faster than most observers expected. He campaigned actively in East Germany's first free elections in March 1990, which produced a landslide for his eastern German CDU partner — a clear mandate for rapid reunification.

Key Fact

The Two Plus Four Treaty (signed 12 September 1990) provided the international framework for reunification. The 'two' were the two German states; the 'four' were the wartime Allies (USA, UK, France, USSR). Germany accepted its existing borders — including the Polish border — and agreed not to develop nuclear weapons. The USSR accepted reunification in exchange for substantial financial compensation and assurances about NATO's future role.

Reunification: 3 October 1990

The Two Plus Four Treaty (Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany) was signed on 12 September 1990. It settled the international dimensions of reunification: Germany's existing borders were confirmed, the occupation rights of the four powers ended, Germany agreed not to develop weapons of mass destruction, and NATO's jurisdiction would not extend to the former GDR territory. Germany was formally reunified on 3 October 1990 — now celebrated as German Unity Day. The GDR ceased to exist; its five eastern states (Länder) joined the Federal Republic of Germany.

The two Germanies that merged in 1990 were very different. East Germany's economy was far weaker than the West's: its industries were uncompetitive, its infrastructure decrepit, and its currency had been exchanged at a politically generous but economically damaging 1:1 rate with the Deutschmark. In the first years after reunification, many East German factories closed, unemployment in the East soared to around 30–40% in some areas, and billions of Deutschmarks of annual transfers flowed from West to East. The psychological gulf — the 'Mauer im Kopf' (wall in the head) — between Easterners and Westerners persisted long after the physical wall had gone. Many East Germans felt their experience, qualifications and way of life had been devalued in the unified Germany.
exam_tip_html: For questions on why the GDR collapsed in 1989, use a multi-causal structure: Gorbachev's reforms (removing Soviet military backstop), the Hungary escape route (showing the Wall could be bypassed), the Monday Demonstrations (internal pressure), and the SED's own confusion (the Schabowski press conference). Don't just say 'the Wall fell' — explain why it fell. For 16-mark period essays on reunification, balance the role of individuals (Gorbachev, Kohl) against structural factors (economic failure of GDR, popular pressure) in your overall judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika reforms from 1985, and his refusal to use Soviet military force in Eastern Europe, removed the GDR's ultimate security guarantee. The 1989 revolutions across Eastern Europe, particularly Hungary's open border in May 1989, accelerated the GDR's crisis.
  • The Monday Demonstrations in Leipzig grew from hundreds in September 1989 to over 100,000 by mid-October. The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989 after a confused SED announcement. Honecker had been ousted in October 1989.
  • Helmut Kohl's Ten-Point Plan (November 1989) drove rapid reunification. The Two Plus Four Treaty (September 1990) provided international approval. Germany was formally reunified on 3 October 1990 — German Unity Day.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Gorbachev's reforms and their impact on East Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks awarded for a developed feature, e.g.:
• Gorbachev's refusal to use Soviet military force to maintain communist governments in Eastern Europe (reversing the Brezhnev Doctrine) meant that the GDR could no longer rely on Soviet tanks to crush popular opposition, making its regime fundamentally vulnerable when protests grew in 1989. [2 marks]
1 mark awarded for simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the events that led to the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Two features identified with basic description.
Secure: Each described with context, e.g.:
• The Monday Demonstrations in Leipzig grew from small prayer meetings in September 1989 to approximately 120,000 demonstrators by mid-October, showing the scale of popular opposition to the SED regime. [2 marks]
• A confused SED press conference announcement on 9 November 1989 by Günter Schabowski led thousands of East Berliners to converge on border crossings; overwhelmed guards opened the gates without clear orders, and the Wall fell. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the GDR collapsed in 1989.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple statement.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Clear analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Analyses the mechanism and relates to wider context.
Example: Gorbachev's decision not to use Soviet military force to save communist regimes in Eastern Europe was decisive. When Hungary opened its border with Austria in May 1989, approximately 30,000 East Germans escaped westward by September — demonstrating that the Wall could now be bypassed. The SED faced a choice between large-scale domestic violence (without Soviet backing) and reform. Neither Honecker nor his replacement Krenz could navigate this dilemma, and the regime collapsed under the weight of its own contradictions.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the fall of the Berlin Wall for Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple identification.
Developing: Some explanation.
Secure: Analytical explanation with evidence.
Mastering: Explores longer-term consequences.
Example: The fall of the Wall made reunification almost inevitable — once East Germans could move freely to the West, the GDR's continued existence as a separate state was difficult to justify. Kohl's Ten-Point Plan of November 1989 turned the political desire for reunification into a practical programme. The March 1990 free elections in East Germany produced a landslide for rapid reunification, and Germany was formally unified on 3 October 1990 — less than a year after the Wall had fallen. The speed of reunification surprised most observers and created significant economic and social challenges for the new unified state.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Helmut Kohl in the reunification of Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Simple description of Kohl's role.
Developing: Some assessment.
Secure: Significance at the time and over time.
Mastering: Weighs Kohl's role against structural factors (Soviet withdrawal, popular pressure, GDR collapse) and argues a nuanced position.
At the time: Ten-Point Plan set the agenda; active campaigning in East Germany's March 1990 elections; negotiation of Two Plus Four Treaty securing international consent.
Over time: Reunification under Kohl set the terms — East German states joined the FRG, not a new shared state, meaning West German institutions were extended eastward; this shaped the successes and difficulties of post-1990 integration.

practice_questions.text:
'Gorbachev's reforms were the main reason why Germany was reunified in 1990.' How far do you agree?
Consider other factors alongside Gorbachev's role and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Mostly descriptive, no judgement.
Developing: Some argument on both sides.
Secure: Balanced argument with evidence; clear overall judgement.
Mastering: Weighs Gorbachev against the GDR's own internal collapse, Kohl's political leadership, popular pressure from the Monday Demonstrations, and international diplomacy (Two Plus Four).

For Gorbachev: Removing the Soviet military backstop made the GDR's collapse possible; without glasnost/perestroika, the political space for 1989 revolutions would not have opened.
Against as most important: Internal GDR collapse (economic failure, emigration crisis, Monday Demonstrations) created the immediate pressure; Kohl's political skill accelerated the process; popular demand in both Germanies drove reunification's speed.

knowledge_checks.q: The Berlin Wall fell on the night of what date in 1989?
The _____ Treaty, signed 12 September 1990, provided the international framework for German reunification.
Germany was formally reunified on 3 October _____, now celebrated as German Unity Day.
Match each person or event to its significance in 1989–1990.
right: Refused to use Soviet military force to save communist regimes
Ten-Point Plan driving German reunification from November 1989
Weekly protests in Leipzig growing to over 100,000 by October 1989

flashcard_questions.a: Gorbachev's policy of openness — greater freedom of expression in the Soviet Union from 1985.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Gorbachev's decisive policy change for Eastern Europe?
flashcard_questions.a: He refused to use Soviet military force to maintain communist governments — reversing the Brezhnev Doctrine.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Hungary's actions in 1989 affect East Germany?
flashcard_questions.a: Hungary opened its border with Austria in May 1989, giving East Germans a new escape route to the West.

flashcard_questions.q: Where did the Monday Demonstrations take place?
flashcard_questions.a: Leipzig, East Germany, beginning at the Nikolaikirche (St Nicholas Church).

flashcard_questions.q: How large did the Monday Demonstrations grow by mid-October 1989?
Why did the Berlin Wall fall on 9 November 1989?
flashcard_questions.a: A confused press conference announcement led thousands to converge on border crossings; overwhelmed guards opened the gates.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Kohl announce his Ten-Point Plan for reunification?
flashcard_questions.a: 28 November 1989 — less than three weeks after the Wall fell.

flashcard_questions.q: What were the 'two' and 'four' in the Two Plus Four Treaty?
flashcard_questions.a: The two German states and the four wartime Allied powers (USA, UK, France, USSR).
The 'wall in the head' — the persistent psychological divide between East and West Germans after physical reunification.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was the 1:1 exchange rate between East and West German marks economically damaging?
flashcard_questions.a: It overvalued East German currency, making East German goods uncompetitive and accelerating factory closures.

glossary_terms.definition: Soviet leader from 1985 who introduced glasnost and perestroika, and crucially refused to use military force to save communist regimes in Eastern Europe in 1989.
Gorbachev's policy of openness — allowing greater freedom of expression and information in the Soviet Union from the mid-1980s.
Gorbachev's policy of economic and political restructuring of the Soviet Union, intended to make it more efficient and competitive.
Weekly peaceful protests in Leipzig from September 1989, growing to over 100,000 demonstrators by October and demanding reform and freedom in East Germany.
Helmut Kohl, CDU Chancellor of West Germany 1982–1998, who drove German reunification through his Ten-Point Plan and the Two Plus Four negotiations.
The treaty signed on 12 September 1990 by the two German states and the four wartime Allies, providing the international legal framework for German reunification.
The 'wall in the head' — the psychological divide between former East and West Germans that persisted long after physical reunification in 1990.
